stories.headline: Colorado secretary of state candidates agree office needs depoliticizing, disagree sharply on how
stories.summary:
The two major-party candidates vying to become Colorado's next secretary of state both say they want to remove politics from election administration, but their visions for the office differ dramatically. Democrat Amanda Gonzalez, currently Jefferson County's clerk and recorder, says she would combat election conspiracies through transparency and pledges to defend Colorado's universal mail voting system. Republican James Wiley, a former executive director of the Colorado Libertarian Party, calls himself an election skeptic and says he wants the office to be 'boring again,' arguing it should not engage in overtly political fights — and he would effectively abolish mail voting.

Three additional candidates are on the Nov. 3 ballot: Libertarian Sean Vadney, who secured a last-minute spot after the party's initial candidate dropped out; Amanda Campbell of the American Constitution Party; and Celeste Landry of the Colorado Forward Party.

The race has drawn heightened attention in an era of intensified scrutiny of election officials. Current Secretary of State Jena Griswold has been a vocal opponent of former President Trump's claims of widespread election fraud, raising the office's national profile. The Secretary of State's Office carries a budget approaching $50 million and oversees business registrations, a voter roll of roughly 4 million Coloradans, campaign finance enforcement, and ballot signature verification.

stories.headline: Denver Mayor Johnston pitches 'childcare for all' by 2031, but funding and logistics remain unresolved
stories.summary:
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston, who recently launched his reelection campaign, has proposed achieving universal childcare for all Denver children under age 4 by 2031. Johnston argues that without intervention, the city risks losing young families to lower cost-of-living metro areas, citing data showing childcare costs can exceed $100,000 over the first three years of a child's life. Childcare experts say no U.S. city has achieved the scale Johnston envisions, though they note Denver has a relatively strong base of early childhood education specialists.

The scope of the challenge is considerable. Denver has nearly 31,000 children under age 4, but existing childcare centers hold only about 5,000 spots staffed by 986 caregivers. More than 8,000 new Denverites are born each year, and available spots carry costs that frequently exceed federal affordability thresholds.

The city's ongoing budget constraints, workforce retention challenges, and shifting political landscape present significant obstacles. Former at-large City Council member Robin Kniech said while it is not surprising to see Johnston aim high, the scale of the proposal is larger than what a city government typically undertakes and lacks clear precedents. Johnston's team has pointed to the city's existing preschool program for 3- and 4-year-olds as a potential foundation, but officials acknowledge a large funding gap remains unresolved.

stories.headline: Colorado Springs Gazette editorial board releases 2026 ballot endorsements ahead of Nov. 3 election
stories.summary:
The Colorado Springs Gazette editorial board released its full slate of recommendations for the Nov. 3 statewide and congressional elections. The board endorsed incumbents in the 5th and 3rd Congressional Districts and backed the local district attorney seeking reelection, citing his stance on public safety and opposition to legislative 'justice reform' policies.

On ballot measures, the Gazette recommended 'yes' votes on a measure requiring law enforcement to report violent offenders to immigration authorities, a measure protecting the right to buy and sell natural gas, a constitutional right to hunt and fish, additional mail ballot security requirements, and a plain-language readability standard for ballot questions. The board also weighed in on congressional redistricting procedures.

The endorsements reflect the conservative editorial stance of the Gazette, one of Colorado's largest newspapers. The Nov. 3 election includes competitive statewide races and several high-profile ballot measures that have drawn significant outside spending and attention from both parties.

stories.headline: Denver man sentenced to 76 years in prison for 2025 murder, armed robbery
stories.summary:
Augustine Vega, 36, was sentenced to 76 years in prison for the March 2025 fatal shooting of 35-year-old David Maffett in the 2900 block of South Vine Street in Denver, the Denver District Attorney's Office announced Friday. Authorities said Vega and the victim appeared to know one another. Hours before the shooting, Vega had robbed a convenience store on South Colorado Boulevard.

After the shooting, Vega drove to Nebraska, where he was arrested by state troopers following a high-speed chase near Gothenburg. Vega and a passenger were found unresponsive in the vehicle after it was stopped; both were given Narcan and transported to hospitals. The passenger later died.

Vega was convicted at trial in August on multiple counts including second-degree murder, aggravated robbery, and burglary. District Attorney John Walsh said the sentence 'makes Denver a safer city by taking Augustine Vega off the streets for decades to come.'

stories.headline: Avalanche roll to 2-0 start with 6-1 rout of Blues; Necas scores twice, Lehkonen shines
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche continued their dominant start to the 2026-27 NHL season Saturday night, defeating the St. Louis Blues 6-1 at Ball Arena to improve to 2-0. Martin Necas scored twice and finished with three points, while Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar each recorded three points. Mackenzie Blackwood was sharp in net with 26 saves.

The Avalanche's top line controlled play from the opening minutes. Makar scored the first goal of the game on a passing sequence involving MacKinnon and Necas, and Colorado built a commanding lead through the first two periods before a pair of goals 23 seconds apart by Nicolas Roy and Necas effectively ended the contest at 6-0. Blues goaltender Jordan Binnington, playing his first start of the season, had a night to forget.

The result follows Colorado's season-opening 8-4 win over the Los Angeles Kings on Wednesday. Artturi Lehkonen, still without a contract for next season, has been a standout with three goals and an assist through the first two games. Coach Jared Bednar said the team improved on nearly every aspect from the opener, praising the squad's skating, energy, and defensive play that consistently led to offensive chances.

stories.headline: Broncos-49ers scouting report: Denver faces undefeated San Francisco in Week 4 road test
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos travel to San Francisco for a Week 4 matchup against the undefeated 49ers, who present one of the NFL's most difficult offensive challenges. Quarterback Brock Purdy has yet to be sacked through three games, leads the league against the blitz with a 155.2 passer rating, and has thrown nine touchdowns against just one interception. However, the 49ers' offensive line has faced two of the worst defensive fronts in the league the past two weeks, and Denver's defense — which generated 24 pressures against the Rams' Matthew Stafford in Week 3 — represents a significant step up in competition.

The Broncos' primary concern entering the game is their struggling offense, particularly in the first half. Denver has been shut out in the first quarter in 16 of 39 games with Bo Nix at quarterback, and Nix has posted four touchdowns, three interceptions, and five sacks through three weeks compared to Purdy's nine touchdowns, one interception, and zero sacks. Denver's running game ranks second-worst in the NFL through three weeks.

Defensively, Colorado has advantages in several matchups. Outside linebacker Nik Bonitto is expected to square off against All-Pro tackle Trent Williams, and Zach Allen is off to a fast start with 12 pressures and three sacks. San Francisco's wide receiver group carries injury concerns, with Mike Evans listed as questionable with a rib injury, though tight end George Kittle and running back Christian McCaffrey remain elite weapons in the middle of the field.

stories.headline: CSU fires defensive coordinator Tyson Summers mid-game in 56-26 loss to Oregon State
stories.summary:
Colorado State head coach Jim Mora relieved defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of his duties during Saturday's 56-26 home loss to Oregon State at Canvas Stadium in Fort Collins, a blowout in which the Beavers compiled 651 yards of total offense. Summers was absent from the sideline after Oregon State's second touchdown of the first quarter. Cornerbacks coach Trent Matthews signaled plays to the defense before co-defensive coordinator Kenny McClendon assumed play-calling duties.

After the game, Mora confirmed Summers is permanently out of the program. McClendon, who came with Mora from UConn and has worked alongside him for five seasons, will take over as the Rams' defensive coordinator. Mora cited McClendon's integrity and experience as reasons for confidence in the transition.

The firing comes after CSU's defense allowed 100 points and more than 1,100 yards in its two preceding games. Summers had been retained by Mora after serving as interim head coach when former CSU coach Jay Norvell was dismissed mid-season last year. Running back Durell Robinson finished with 117 yards and a touchdown for the Rams, but the performance could not offset the defensive collapse as CSU fell to 2-3 in its first season in the Pac-12 Conference.

stories.headline: Adam 12 Five Star Schools board to vote on closure and consolidation plan Wednesday
stories.summary:
The Board of Education for Adam 12 Five Star Schools, a suburban district serving communities north of Denver including Northglenn and Thornton, is expected to vote Wednesday on a closure and consolidation plan. The proposal reflects broader pressures facing suburban school districts, including enrollment declines and budget constraints.

Details of which specific schools face closure or consolidation were not immediately available, but the vote represents a significant decision for families and staff in the district. Adam 12 serves tens of thousands of students across Adams County.

stories.headline: Nosu Ramen closes in Golden after six-year run; Sakura Bowl also shutters in Centennial
stories.summary:
Nosu Ramen has permanently closed its Golden location after six years in business, owner Brandon Bortles confirmed to Westword. Bortles cited a combination of rising operating costs, changing economic conditions, and financial pressures that made renewing the restaurant's lease unsustainable. The restaurant opened in February 2020 and was almost immediately hit with pandemic-era mandatory closures, creating an ongoing financial headwind.

Bortles also owns the Cherry Creek restaurant Abejas, which has temporarily closed due to what he described as a 'building issue.' He said financial, insurance, and legal matters preclude him from discussing details. Separately, Sakura Bowl in Centennial also closed after 15 years, with ownership citing personal reasons.

In other Denver-area restaurant news, chef Johnny Curiel announced that Tequilería Alteño — which launched as a summer pop-up at the Clayton Hotel in Cherry Creek — will permanently replace Mar Bella Wine Bar. The restaurant is temporarily closing for a remodel, with a spring or summer 2027 reopening planned. Additionally, Slice House, the fast-casual pizza chain from world pizza champion Tony Gemignani, delayed the opening of its Longmont location past its planned September date to complete finishing work and staff training.

stories.headline: Stanley Hotel in Estes Park named one of USA Today's 10 best haunted hotels
stories.summary:
The Stanley Hotel in Estes Park has earned a spot on USA Today's 10Best list of the nation's top haunted hotels, placing tenth. The publication described the 'dramatic, massive, white hotel' as appearing to rise out of the Colorado mountains. The Stanley is widely known as the inspiration for Stephen King's novel 'The Shining.'

The honor was determined by a reader vote following nominations by an expert panel. The hotel offers a variety of tours highlighting its most storied and reportedly haunted locations. Estes Park, situated at the gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park, draws significant tourism in autumn, and the recognition is expected to bolster interest ahead of the Halloween season.

stories.headline: Children's Museum of Denver to host Harvest Hoot Halloween event Oct. 23-25
stories.summary:
The Children's Museum of Denver at Marsico Campus will host its 'Harvest Hoot' event from Oct. 23 through Oct. 25. The multi-day event will feature the Monster Mash Circus and Adventure Forest, along with activities including sensory sand potion-making, carnival games, spooky stuffed animal crafting, and a cranberry bog exploration.

All Harvest Hoot activities are included with standard museum admission, and members attend free. Tickets must be purchased at the museum on the day of the visit, as advance tickets are not available. Families are encouraged to come in costumes, provided they are family-friendly.

topStory.headline: Trump Campaigns Across Midwest Ahead of Midterms as Approval Ratings Sink, Party Faces Headwinds
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump held rallies in Ohio and Oklahoma this week as part of a planned 32-day campaign blitz aimed at bolstering Republican candidates ahead of November midterm elections. At a Saturday rally in Vandalia, Ohio, Trump told supporters there would be a "big surprise" on election day and urged them to turn out to vote, saying, "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big." Trump campaigned specifically for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, among others.

Husted faces a competitive race against Democrat Sherrod Brown and hopes Trump's appearance will energize Republican base voters who might otherwise skip a midterm election. Husted told reporters he believes the United States must win the ongoing war with Iran "on our terms" and emphasized he is "fighting for lower prices" for constituents. Trump used a significant portion of his rally remarks to defend data centers and AI infrastructure investment in Ohio, an issue that has become politically contentious amid bipartisan voter concerns over electricity costs, farmland use, and water consumption.

Trump's political standing has deteriorated since his 2024 presidential election victory, when he captured more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote. Ohio gasoline prices have risen 35 percent over the past year to an average of $4.16 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association, and Trump's trade policies have triggered retaliatory Canadian tariffs affecting roughly $3 billion in Ohio exports. His national approval rating has reached an all-time low, with voters expressing frustration over the cost of living, the Iran war, and immigration enforcement actions.

Some Republican strategists have openly questioned whether Trump's high-visibility campaigning helps or hurts the party's chances. Political strategist Steve Schmidt said Trump's rallies have become "his lead weight" and that "the American people are sick and tired of him," arguing the midterm elections are fundamentally a referendum on the president. Despite those concerns, Trump allies and rally attendees say the events remain energizing for supporters and serve as a direct line between the president and the Republican base. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress, and the midterm results will determine whether the party retains control of the legislative branch for the remainder of Trump's term.
